source.title: Robusto-1 Dataset: Comparing Humans and VLMs on Real Out-Of-Distribution Autonomous Driving VQA from Peru
source.authors: Dunant Cusipuma; David Ortega; Victor Flores-Benites; Arturo Deza

record.tranche_reason: The study reports partial and question-dependent similarity between human and VLM answer patterns, and argues that similarity among VLMs may relate to shared training data. It uses RSA on answer embeddings, not a scale sweep or internal model representations.
record.gate_note: Rows record RSA, distance-to-median, and PCA results on answer embeddings. The authors caution that similar answers do not establish similar internal representations. The paper also cites prior work, which is not recorded as study results.
record.test_reason: The study embeds the text answers of 6 VLMs and 9 humans and compares them with RSA, distance to the median and PCA. That is behavioural output similarity, not similarity of model representations. The authors say similar answers do not imply aligned internal representations. There is no scale sweep, no image-caption pairing, no seed comparison, no mapping or stitching, no feature analysis, and no comparison of representation metrics. This is a related but different construct, so it tests no version. The Platonic Representation Hypothesis is cited only in the discussion.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors find that alignment varies strongly by question type. VLMs answer very alike ('All VLMs are alike, each Human is different'), while human–VLM alignment is mild. They speculate that shared internet training data and Transformer architectures explain VLM similarity. They stress that similar answers are necessary but not sufficient evidence of representational alignment.
record.recipe_differences: Uses RSA on sentence embeddings of answers to driving questions and compares humans with six VLMs; it does not compare internal network representations across model scales or perform a scale sweep.
record.method_sensitivity: Similarity patterns vary by question block. Alternative sentence embeddings preserve the reported pattern but change its intensity; pooling responses appears to increase VLM convergence relative to single responses.

fits_no_version.finding: Six VLMs from different developers (Gemini, Llama, Pixtral, Qwen2, CogVLM, DeepSeek) give highly similar answer patterns (answer-embedding RSA) on 105 OOD driving VQA items, across all question blocks. Human answers diverge, especially on counterfactuals, and human–VLM alignment is mild. The result holds across 3 sentence embedders and with single or pooled responses; pooling increases apparent VLM convergence.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Behavioural (output) convergence: different VLMs produce more similar answers to one another than humans do to each other or to VLMs.

record.peer_reviewed: 2025 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition Workshops (CVPRW)
record.problems: Small pilot: 9 human participants, 6 VLMs, and 7 held-out videos. Results are mainly qualitative descriptions of plots without numerical RSA or distance values. The measurements use embeddings of model answers, not internal model representations; model inputs and frame processing also differ, and the authors note that PCA overlap can be misleading.
record.rows_left_out: No additional relevant results left out.

untested.parts: No size or capability sweep and no internal representations.
No alignment of paired image-caption representations.
No mapping, stitching or relative-representation tests.
No feature, neuron or circuit analysis.
No variation of a similarity metric on model representations. The embedder and pooling checks apply to answer embeddings only.
No measure of representational alignment, and no causal test of shared data. The shared-data explanation is speculation.

record.verdict_notes: Small pilot: 9 humans, 6 VLMs, 7 videos, and no numerical RSA values in the text. Inputs are confounded across models: frame rates differ (0.5 to 10 fps), Llama sees only 3 frames, and DeepSeek processes images only for OCR (pseudo-multimodal). Many VLM multiple-choice answers were curated (31.75% modified). The GPT question-generation prompt in the text is study material and was not followed.

versions.untested_parts: No model size or capability sweep, nor comparison of alignment across scale.
No paired image-caption alignment comparison or scaling of vision and language models.
No same-architecture, different-seed comparison of features or shared subspaces.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation, or unpaired interchangeability test.
No recurring interpretable features, neurons, or circuits are tested.

The study varies question block and reports robustness across sentence embeddings and answer pooling choices. It does not test neighbour-count settings, other OOD datasets, or internal model-representation metrics.
No scale-related plateau is tested, and shared data or objectives are not causally isolated from other explanations.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: Answer-pattern similarity varies by question type: human similarity is high on multiple-choice questions and nearly absent on counterfactual/hypothetical questions, while human–VLM answer distances also differ by block (r4–r9).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The broad RSA pattern remains across sentence embeddings and single versus pooled responses, although its intensity changes and pooling appears to increase VLM convergence (r13–r16).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: VLM and human answer patterns on the tested driving questions
reader_labels.reason: The authors report only mild human–VLM alignment, with the greatest answer-pattern difference on counterfactual/hypothetical questions; their results concern a small answer-embedding study rather than internal representations (r7–r9).
